look_here_first: Look at the leaf dissection and overall slenderness first: lower leaves are often deeply pinnatifid, while the upper flowering branches become narrow and simple; the plant is much less gray-woolly than Verbena canescens.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts Verbena halei and lists Texas within its native range. Hays County — the project Hays County native-source list includes Verbena halei. Travis County — the University of Texas Plant Resources Center Travis County Verbenaceae index includes a Verbena halei herbarium specimen. Kerr County — the Kerr Wildlife Management Area vascular flora documents Verbena halei without an introduced marker.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Do not use cultivated/native-plant-sale listings as county evidence. User iNaturalist observations support encounter/photo value but are not required for the range decision.

best_field_traits: slender perennial, usually one to a few stems with an open branched flowering canopy
lower leaves variable but often deeply pinnately lobed or cut
upper leaves become much narrower, simpler, and sometimes nearly entire
stems comparatively sparsely hairy rather than densely gray-canescent
slender terminal/branched spikes with widely spaced tiny lavender-purple flowers
four-angled to ridged stems; opposite leaves
fruit breaks into four one-seeded mericarps
morphology_keys.verbena_training: Separate these by leaf architecture + hair texture + spike/branching architecture before using flower color.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Verbena canescens: Gray vervain is shorter and densely gray-hairy/canescent over stems and leaves; Texas vervain is more slender and comparatively greener/less hairy, with more deeply divided lower leaves. Verbena xutha: Gulf vervain is coarser, more strongly hispid/glandular, and typically has conspicuous 3-lobed leaves rather than the slender highly variable pinnatifid-to-linear leaf progression of V. halei. Verbena scabra: Sandpaper vervain is much more robust, with broad rough ovate leaves and long coarse spikes.
